source_text:
ἵνα δὲ μὴ τὴν ἐντολὴν ἢ τὸν ταύτην δεδωκότα θεὸν αἰτιάσωνταί τινες, γείτονι καὶ ὁμοσπόρῳ ἐχρήσατο ῥήματι τοιάδε φάσκων· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ὁ νόμος ἅγιος καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ
ἀγαθή. Ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἡ ἁμαρτία, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ διάβολος, φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν, ἐπιφέρει λέγων· ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερ 4 βολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς. τὸ γὰρ κατ' οὐσίαν τὶ ὂν τὸ πλέον καὶ τὸ ἔλαττον οὐκ ἐπιδέξεται· ἔστιν γὰρ ὅπερ ἐστίν, ἀεὶ τοῦτο ὂν ὅπερ ἐστὶν οὐσιωδῶς. τῷ γὰρ γινομένῳ καὶ ἐπιγινομένῳ τι, εἴτε ὀλίγον εἴτε καθ' ὑπερβολήν, ἕτερός ἐστι κατ' οὐσίαν τῶν αὐτῷ ἐπιγινομένων· τὸ γὰρ πόσον οὐκ οὐσία ἀλλὰ περὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἐστίν, οὐκ ὂν οὐσία. ἡ ἄρα τοίνυν καλουμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀποστόλου ἁμαρτία τὸ πλέον ἐπιδεχομένη ἁμαρτήσειν, ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία. ἄρα καὶ τοῦ εἶναι ἁμαρτία, ᾗ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν, ἀρχὴν ἔλαβεν, οὐκ οὖσα καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἐν ἀρχῇ κατὰ τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία. διὸ δὴ καὶ τὴν ἐπίτασιν τοῦ γενέσθαι καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸν ἐσομένῳ χρόνῳ σημαίνει οὕτω λέγων· ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς. εἰ δὲ λέγοιεν· καὶ πῶς ἂν εἴη ἀγαθὴ καὶ δικαία; πῶς δὲ ἁγία ἡ ἐντολὴ καὶ ὁ νόμος, ὁπότε διὰ τῆς ἀφορμῆς αὐτῶν 2 ἁμαρτωλὸς καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἐγένετο ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία; πρὸς ταῦτα ἀκουέτωσαν ὅτι οὐκ, εἴ τι καταβλάπτεται, ἤδη καὶ ἡ ἀφορμὴ δι' ἣν βλάπτεται φαύλη ἐστὶ καὶ πονηρά· οὐδὲ γὰρ ὅτι οἱ ἀνόδως καὶ ἀμέτρως ἐνατενίζοντες τῷ ἡλίῳ βλάπτονται τὰς ὄψεις, ἤδη καὶ τὸν ἥλιόν φαμεν πονηρόν· οὐδ' ὅτι καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ὁ διάβολος ἁμαρτωλὸς γέγονε τῷ ἐπικεχειρηκέναι κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἤδη καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ φαῦλον καὶ πονηρὸν εἶναι λέγομεν. Οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοί, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, ἀγαθόν. νῦν εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται. καὶ ὅτι στερηθεὶς τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ, ἀντὶ τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς θάνατον καταλλαξάμενος–καὶ γὰρ θάνατος οὐχ ὁ κοινὸς μόνος τῶν μελῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκράτησεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ τῆς παρακοῆς κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ εἰσβαλών· μάλιστα γὰρ ὁ κρατῶν θάνατος πρὸ τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίας ἐβασίλευσε, κατὰ πάντων νόμον καὶ σκῆπτρον τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βασιλείας ἔχων τὴν παρακοήν. ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄναρχος ἢ ἀγέννητος ἡ τοῦ θανάτου βασιλεία· ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα. τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ· ὃ γὰρ θέλω ἀγαθὸν τοῦτο οὐ ποιῶ, ἀλλ' ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο πράσσω. εἰ τὸ θέλειν μόνον ἐν ἡμῖν ἔστιν, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ θεληθὲν καλὸν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν, εἰς μάτην ὁ ἀγαθὸς θεὸς τὰς ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὰς ἐν τοῖς σώμασι κατέπεμψεν· τὸ γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ αὐταῖς φίλον οὐ πράττουσιν, οὐκ ἐνεργοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ μόνον θέλουσιν· τάχα δὲ οὐδ' αὐτό, ἄδηλον γάρ.
thought_title: The commandment is not to blame; sin is not a substance
orientation: Eusebius is defending the goodness of the law and commandment against those who would blame them for sin, and is beginning to interpret Romans 7 into the person of Adam.
pass_a_gloss: But so that some might not blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying such things: 'But we know that the law is holy and the commandment is holy and just and good.' Since therefore not even sin itself, that is the devil, is sin by nature and substance, he brings in saying: 'so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.' For that which is something according to substance will not admit the more and the less; for it is what it is, always being what it is substantially. For to that which comes to be and to that which comes upon something, whether little or beyond measure, is other in substance than the things that come upon it; for quantity is not substance but is around the substance, not being substance. Therefore then the thing called sin by the apostle, admitting the more in sinning, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure. Therefore also of being sin, in which it is sin, it took a beginning, sin not being in the beginning beyond measure according to the having sinned sinful. Wherefore indeed also the increase of becoming beyond measure sinful in time to come he signifies, saying thus: 'so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.' But if they should say: 'And how would the commandment and the law be good and just? And how holy, when through their occasion sin became sinful beyond measure?' To these things let them hear that not, if something is harmed, is already also the occasion through which it is harmed base and evil; for neither because those who gaze at the sun without pain and without measure are harmed in their eyes, do we already say the sun is evil; nor because the devil became sinful beyond measure by having plotted against the Son of God, do we already say the Son of God is base and evil. 'But I know that good does not dwell in me, that is in my flesh.' Now he interprets into the person of Adam. And that having been deprived of having God in himself, having exchanged death for the truly real life—for not only the common death of his members mastered him, but also the death of disobedience entering against his soul; for especially the mastering death reigned before the coming of Christ, having disobedience as law and scepter of its own kingdom against all. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for from the living the having died comes about, and from the obedience of the obedient the disobeying of someone. 'For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good is not; for what good I will, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice.' If the willing alone is in us, but the working out of the willed good is not in us, in vain did the good God send down the souls of the same substance as himself into bodies; for what is dear to him and to them they do not practice, they do not work, but only will; and perhaps not even this, for it is unclear.

choices.english: he used a neighboring and kindred word
choices.why: Literal rendering preserves the metaphor of a word close in meaning and family to the commandment, matching the source's spatial and kinship imagery.
The glossary bans 'sin-nature' and 'sinful power'; this literal phrase keeps the quantitative language Eusebius is analyzing.

choices.term: τὸ πλέον καὶ τὸ ἔλαττον οὐκ ἐπιδέξεται
choices.english: will not admit the more and the less
choices.why: Literal philosophical language about substance and quantity; 'admit' preserves the technical sense of receiving degrees.
rejected: does not allow increase or decrease

choices.why: The source has two adverbs; literal rendering keeps the paired adverbial force and the odd 'without pain' reading.
Literal rendering of παράκειταί as 'lies beside' preserves the spatial metaphor of something present but not active.
rejected: the willing is present with me

choices.english: the souls of the same substance as himself
choices.why: Literal rendering of ὁμοουσίας keeps the theological weight of the term without importing later creedal language.

pass_b_english: But so that no one would blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying: "We know that the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good" (Romans 7:12). Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is not sin by nature or substance, he brings in the next statement: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). For what exists as a substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is in its substance. But for something that comes into being and has things come upon it—whether little or beyond measure—it is other in substance than the things that come upon it. For quantity is not substance but is around substance, not being substance itself. Therefore the one called sin by the apostle, since it admits the more in its sinning, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure—this one also received a beginning of being sin, in the way that it is sin, not being sinful beyond measure in the beginning according to its having sinned. This is why he indicates the increase of its becoming sinful beyond measure in a time to come, saying: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just? How could they be holy, when through the occasion they provided sin became sinful beyond measure? Let them hear in response that it is not the case that if something is harmed, the occasion through which it is harmed is already base and evil. For it is not because those who gaze at the sun immoderately and without measure are harmed in their eyes that we call the sun evil; nor is it because the devil became sinful beyond measure by having plotted against the Son of God that we say the Son of God is base and evil. "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh" (Romans 7:18). Now he interprets this into the person of Adam. And because he was deprived of having God in himself, he exchanged death for true life—for not only did the common death of his members seize him, but also the death of disobedience entered against his soul. For the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ, holding disobedience as the law and scepter of its kingdom over all. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying comes from the living, and one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey. "For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not" (Romans 7:18). "For the good I want, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice" (Romans 7:19). If the willing alone is in us, and the working out of the good that is willed is not in us, then the good God sent the souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain. For what is dear to him and to them they do not do; they do not enact it, but only will it—and perhaps not even that, for it is unclear.
notes: The source has 'καθ' ὑπερ 4 βολὴν' with a line break and numeral 4 inserted, likely a page or column number in the manuscript; the text is read as καθ' ὑπερβολήν.
The source has 'αὐτῶν 2 ἁμαρτωλὸς' with a numeral 2 inserted, likely a page or column number; the text is read as αὐτῶν ἁμαρτωλὸς.

problems.source_quote: ἀνόδως καὶ ἀμέτρως ἐνατενίζοντες τῷ ἡλίῳ
problems.why: ἀνόδως means 'immoderately/excessively', not 'without pain'. The point is gazing too much, not painlessly.
problems.fix: immoderately and without measure gaze at the sun
problems.ruling: Greek ἀνόδως = excessive, not 'without pain'; translation changes the nuance of the argument.

fixed: Changed 'without pain and without measure' to 'immoderately and without measure' because ἀνόδως means 'immoderately/excessively', not 'without pain'.

problems.quote: For what exists as a substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is in its substance.
problems.why: Tautological repetition obscures philosophical point about substance vs. accident.
problems.fix: Substances do not admit of more or less; they are what they are absolutely.

problems.quote: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
problems.why: Archaic/ungrammatical: 'the willing' as noun, 'lies beside me' obscure.
problems.fix: 'To will is present with me, but to do the good is not' (RSV-style).

problems.quote: then the good never was and never will be in human life, and no one ever enacted it
problems.why: Missing logical connector: 'if they take...as' leaves conditional hanging.
problems.fix: Add 'But if they take...then they must conclude...'

problems.quote: the common death of his members
problems.why: Three different 'death' expressions in one paragraph; unclear if same or different.
problems.fix: Clarify whether all three refer to the same death or distinct aspects.

variants.text: the common death of his members

problems.quote: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just?
problems.why: Unclear who 'they' are—opponents? imagined objectors? Not previously introduced.
problems.fix: Specify: 'if opponents object' or 'if someone asks'.

problems.quote: dying comes from the living, and one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
problems.why: Logically backwards: disobedience from obedience makes no sense as written.
problems.fix: Likely 'obedience comes from disobedience' or needs retranslation.

problems.quote: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
problems.why: 'The willing' as a noun phrase is not natural English; meaning is opaque.
problems.fix: Render as 'the desire to do good is present in me' or similar.

problems.quote: he voted with it as holy and just and good
problems.why: 'Voted' is a modern political word; likely means 'he testified' or 'he assented.'
problems.fix: Replace with 'he testified' or 'he declared it'.

edits.old: For what exists as a substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is in its substance.
edits.new: For what exists as a substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is substantially.

edits.old: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
edits.new: For to will is present with me, but to work out the good is not

edits.old: dying comes from the living, and one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
edits.new: dying comes from the living, and one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey

fixed: Substance vs. accident: the English 'always being what it is in its substance' is a fair rendering of 'ἀεὶ τοῦτο ὂν ὅπερ ἐστὶν οὐσιωδῶς'; no change needed beyond minor wording.
The willing: 'τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι' is better rendered as 'to will is present with me'; changed.
Missing logical connector: the reported sentence 'then the good never was...' does not appear in the current English; no edit possible.
Common death of his members: 'ὁ κοινὸς μόνος τῶν μελῶν αὐτοῦ' means the common death of his members; the English is accurate.
They: 'εἰ δὲ λέγοιεν' is an indefinite 'if they should say'; the English is accurate.
Disobedience from obedience: the source says 'ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα'—disobedience comes from the obedience of the obedient; the English is accurate.
The willing: same as above; changed.
Voted: the reported sentence does not appear in the current English; no edit possible.

last_rejected.quote: one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα
last_rejected.why: Source says disobedience comes FROM obedience of those who obey; English reverses the causal direction.
last_rejected.fix: and disobedience by someone comes from the obedience of those who obey
last_rejected.ruling: Greek says disobedience comes from obedience; English matches this direction.

last_rejected.quote: "For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not" (Romans 7:18).

last_rejected.why: The Greek passage is Romans 7:22, not 7:18; the citation is incorrect.
last_rejected.fix: "For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not" (Romans 7:22).
